{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-mo-f","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"bbc4929d9b9546c49acfd71ecaca1c1fb4bbeb3911071cd52d4f38000432f249","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-mo-class-f:lineage:28","source_registry_sha256":"f128002157e581eb7004b9370c8cfbafd7b29a1596262980704fbda0a45932f5","source_liveness_sha256":"fdf72d02e75b9589fee5aaf5b83ec9705ff03586f574464e3553a827f9b698d8"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Missouri highway driving: lane choice, speed control, passing and being passed, matching traffic, stopping, ramps, interchanges, highway hypnosis, drowsiness and breakdowns","heading":"C — Highway driving: staying alert, choosing the proper lane, controlling speed, passing and blind spots, being passed, adjusting to traffic, stopping, entering and leaving controlled access highways, interchanges, highway hypnosis, sleepiness and breakdown emergencies","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Highway driving: staying alert, choosing the proper lane, controlling speed, passing and blind spots, being passed, adjusting to traffic, stopping, entering and leaving controlled access highways, interchanges, highway hypnosis, sleepiness and breakdown emergencies
Knowledge domain: how to scan and stay alert on the highway, which lane to use on two-lane and multi-lane roads, how to pass, be passed and blend with traffic speed, where and how to stop, how to use entrance and exit ramps and interchanges, how to fight highway hypnosis and fatigue, and what to do after a breakdown.

FACT_ID: sec07-F01 | anchor: A01
Keep scanning ahead, to the sides and behind, and never look away from the road for more than a few seconds; to study a map, first pull safely off the road. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F02 | anchor: A01
On a highway with one lane each way, drive in the right lane, crossing the center line to pass only when no oncoming vehicle is near and there is no solid yellow line. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F03 | anchor: A01
On a highway with two or more lanes each way, stay right except to pass slower traffic, make room for a merging driver, or set up a legal left turn. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F04 | anchor: A01
Control your speed by checking the speedometer often and watching posted limits, especially after leaving a fast road for much slower local streets. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F05 | anchor: A01
The left lane is for passing only, the right lane may be used to pass a vehicle turning left, and the shoulder or unpaved edge must never be used for passing. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F06 | anchor: A01
Before passing on a four-lane highway, check the left lane with your left and inside mirrors and take a quick look over your left shoulder. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F07 | anchor: A01
A blind spot is an area your rearview mirrors cannot show, which is why a glance over the shoulder is needed before changing lanes. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F08 | anchor: A01
Avoid riding just behind and to either side of another vehicle; speed up or drop back so its driver can see you. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F09 | anchor: A01
When passing, move through the other driver's blind spot as fast as you can without going over the speed limit. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F10 | anchor: A02
Do not linger beside or right behind a truck or bus, whose large blind spots hide you; if the trucker's face is not visible in the side mirror, you are not visible to the trucker. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec07-F11 | anchor: A02
If the way is clear, signal the lane change, then pass quickly and smoothly without exceeding the limit. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec07-F12 | anchor: A02
Return to the right lane only once the passed vehicle shows in your rearview mirror, after a look over your right shoulder and a signal. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec07-F13 | anchor: A02
When someone starts to pass you, hold your lane and do not speed up. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec07-F14 | anchor: A02
If many drivers are passing you on the right in a multi-lane road, you are likely slower than traffic and should move right when clear unless a left turn is coming up. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec07-F15 | anchor: A02
Crashes involving two or more vehicles often happen when one driver goes faster or slower than the others, so keep pace with traffic. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec07-F16 | anchor: A02
Speeding saves no more than a few minutes an hour, and each pass you make adds another chance of a collision. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec07-F17 | anchor: A02
Driving much slower than traffic is also dangerous; if a line of vehicles builds behind you, pull over when safe and let them by. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec07-F18 | anchor: A02
Check your rearview mirrors every few seconds to track traffic coming up behind you. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec07-F19 | anchor: A02
Spot slow vehicles early, such as heavy trucks and underpowered cars on steep grades or merging, so you can change lanes or ease off instead of braking suddenly. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec07-F20 | anchor: A03
Never stop in the travel lanes of a highway; use rest stops and service areas instead. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec07-F21 | anchor: A03
Look far enough ahead to avoid panic stops, because hard braking can cost you control and makes it harder for drivers behind to stop. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec07-F22 | anchor: A03
In an emergency you may stop on the shoulder; turn on your emergency flashers, and raising the hood or tying a white cloth to the antenna also helps. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec07-F23 | anchor: A03
A controlled access highway lets you get on or off only at entrance and exit ramps. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec07-F24 | anchor: A03
Use the entrance ramp and its acceleration lane to reach the speed of highway traffic, then signal and merge smoothly into a gap. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec07-F25 | anchor: A03
Stopping where the acceleration lane ends is only for very heavy traffic that leaves you no choice. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec07-F26 | anchor: A03
Drivers on the highway should make room for you, but if they do not, you must yield to them rather than force your way in, even if that means stopping. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec07-F27 | anchor: A03
Move into the correct lane well before the deceleration lane, then use that lane and the exit ramp to slow down, obeying the ramp's advisory speed sign. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec07-F28 | anchor: A03
If you miss your exit, never stop, back up or turn around on the highway; take the next exit and come back. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec07-F29 | anchor: A04
On a Diverging Diamond Interchange you drive on the left side of the road for a short stretch, and directional signs at every interchange help you find your way. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec07-F30 | anchor: A04
Highway hypnosis is a drowsy, unaware state caused by the sameness of the road and traffic and the steady hum of wind, tires and engine. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec07-F31 | anchor: A04
Prevent highway hypnosis by keeping your eyes moving over traffic and signs, and leave the highway if you start to feel sleepy. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec07-F32 | anchor: A04
A drowsy driver decides and reacts more slowly and can be as dangerous as a drunk one, so stop at the nearest rest area or service area and nap if very sleepy. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec07-F33 | anchor: A04
After a breakdown, make sure other drivers can see you and your vehicle, since crashes happen when a stalled car is noticed too late. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec07-F34 | anchor: A05
Report a breakdown with a two-way radio or phone; road signs may list a CB channel or number, and the cellphone emergency number is *55. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec07-F35 | anchor: A05
With vehicle trouble, get off the road and away from traffic if at all possible, and turn on your emergency flashers. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec07-F36 | anchor: A05
If you cannot leave the roadway, stop where others can clearly see you, not just past a hill crest or around a curve. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec07-F37 | anchor: A05
Set emergency flares behind a disabled vehicle to warn drivers to change lanes. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec07-F38 | anchor: A05
Never stand in the roadway or change a tire from inside a traffic lane; signal trouble by lifting the hood or tying a white cloth to the antenna, side mirror or door handle. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0043]

Misconceptions: the left lane of a multi-lane highway is not a cruising lane but a passing lane; you do not speed up when someone passes you; a missed exit is never fixed by backing up; driving far below the flow of traffic is not automatically safer.
Mnemonics: mirror, shoulder, signal before every lane change; see the passed car in the mirror before you move back.
Glossary: blind spot means an area around a vehicle that its mirrors do not show; controlled access highway means a road entered and left only by ramps; acceleration lane means the lane at the end of an entrance ramp for building up speed; deceleration lane means the lane before an exit ramp for slowing down; highway hypnosis means drowsy inattention caused by monotonous highway driving.
Dynamic facts: the emergency cellphone number and the CB channel or phone numbers posted along roads are set by authorities and can change, so the posted signs and current Highway Patrol guidance control.
